docs.title: AI Engineering Handbook
docs.text:
Build Document Assistant, an application that answers questions about documents, cites its sources, and asks for approval before it saves a note. You will start with a Python script and finish by reviewing how the system would run on Azure.

Start with Python Browse the roadmap

docs.title: Start here
docs.text: You need a terminal, a text editor, and Python 3.11 or later to run the core examples. If you can already build and test a Python API, start with LLM engineering. For document search, begin with ingestion.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
Stage What Document Assistant learns to do Python and FastAPI Accept a question, validate a request, and stream an answer Models and RAG Work within a context budget and cite authorized source material Tools and agents Propose a typed action, pause for approval, and record the outcome Azure and operations Choose services, promote a release, and diagnose quality and reliability failures

Use one question as a running test

Ask “How many days do I have to return an unopened headset?” Rerun the question as you add retrieval, citations, authentication, and evaluation. Then ask about a policy missing from the sample documents. The system should make its uncertainty visible.

docs.title: How to use the chapters
docs.text: Read the problem and run the main example. Predict what will happen in the debugging exercise before looking at the expected result. Core lessons build applied AI skills. Supporting lessons teach the infrastructure you need to reason about an AI application. Optional sections cover specialized tools and hosted services.

docs.title: Learning roadmap
docs.text:
Follow the sidebar in order or use the prerequisites in each chapter to jump in. Budget about 29 hours for reading and core exercises, with extra time for optional experiments. The numbers below are approximate.

Part Start here Practice goal Time I. Foundations Build a Python CLI Explain the path from a command to a model API call 2.5 hours II. Backend Expose a typed API Validate requests, stream results, and enforce data ownership 3.5 hours III. LLM engineering Budget tokens and build prompts Specify, validate, and measure model behavior 3.5 hours IV. RAG Ingest documents and build chunks Retrieve and cite evidence, then measure where retrieval fails 4.25 hours V. Agents Build a deterministic tool workflow Bound a tool loop and approve a write 4 hours VI. Containers and Azure Package the API with Docker Explain the path from image to a secure cloud request 2 hours VII. Delivery Describe infrastructure with Terraform Review a plan and promote or roll back a revision 2 hours VIII. Production AI Observe quality, latency and cost Diagnose incidents and plan safe improvements 5 hours IX. Capstone Review the production design Defend the design with test evidence and a runbook 2 hours

docs.title: Choose the right depth
docs.text:
Core chapters ask you to build and debug. Supporting chapters ask you to use a tool or explain how it affects your system. Optional material helps you recognize when to consult specialists, for example for cluster administration, enterprise networking, multi-region recovery, or GPU inference optimization.

The progression follows a single application so that every new component addresses a problem you have already seen. Use the roadmaps for further practice after completing a part. FastAPI Tutorial, AI Engineer Roadmap, AI Agents Roadmap

docs.title: From your shell to an HTTP request
docs.text:
Trace the path from your editor and shell to a service on another machine. These checks help you locate failures before you debug Python or the model.

Supporting · 50 minutes · Prerequisites Build a Python CLI.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Two people run the same code and see different results. One has a different Python interpreter. The other cannot reach the API hostname. Identify which boundary failed first.

docs.title: Isolate your environment
docs.text:
Create a virtual environment. It gives this project its own package installation directory.

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip --version

On Bash, use .venv/bin/python. Expect both paths to point into .venv. Calling pip through Python reduces the chance of installing packages into a different interpreter. A dependency file makes the environment easier to recreate.

Use git status --short and git diff in a Git checkout before you commit. The first command shows affected paths. The second shows the tracked edits. Keep credentials in environment variables or a managed secret store. Commit the names of required settings so others can configure their own environment.

docs.title: Trace one request
docs.text:
A process is a running program. A server process listens on a port. DNS resolves a hostname to an address, TCP connects to a destination, TLS authenticates the HTTPS endpoint and encrypts the connection, and HTTP gives the request its method, path, headers, and body.

flowchart LR
    Shell --> Python
    Python --> DNS
    Python -->|HTTPS request| API
    API -->|status and JSON| Python

Use curl.exe -I https://example.com/ on PowerShell or curl -I https://example.com/ on Bash to inspect an HTTP HEAD response. A status line means the request reached an HTTP server or intermediary. A URL with an invalid hostname, such as https://assistant.invalid/, should fail to resolve on a direct connection. A proxy can produce its own error response in either case.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text:
If localhost refuses a connection, use Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen on PowerShell or ss -ltn on Linux to check whether anything is listening. Use Get-Process or ps to identify the process. Check file permissions before diagnosing a permission error as a network issue. An HTTP 401 means a server or gateway responded and you can move on to credentials.

Start with the failing boundary

Record the command, interpreter, host, port, and error. Leave authorization headers and secret values out of your notes.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can distinguish an environment, DNS, connection, TLS, or HTTP failure. Next: Make a model call

Python virtual environments, HTTP semantics, Git status

docs.title: Make a model call
docs.text:
Replace the CLI's echo with a model interface. Start with a fixture and optionally send the same question to a deployed model in Microsoft Foundry.

Core · 55 minutes · Prerequisites The first two foundations chapters. The default example uses Python only.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Model requests have credentials, latency, and variable output. The rest of Document Assistant needs a predictable way to ask a question while we learn how to handle those moving parts.

docs.title: Run a fixture first
docs.text:
A fixture is a known input or response used to exercise code. The fixture lets you check the CLI without sending a request over the network.

"""Ask a fixture or a deployed Azure OpenAI model the same question."""

import argparse
import os

from examples.cli import answer as validate_question


def ask(question: str, *, hosted: bool = False) -> str:
    validate_question(question)
    if not hosted:
        return "Fixture response: use a source document to verify the answer."

    from openai import OpenAI

    resource = os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"].rstrip("/")
    with OpenAI(
        base_url=f"{resource}/openai/v1/",
        api_key=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY"],
        timeout=15,
        max_retries=0,
    ) as client:
        response = client.responses.create(
            model=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT"],
            input=question,
            instructions="Answer briefly and say when you are unsure.",
            max_output_tokens=250,
            store=False,
        )
        if response.status != "completed" or not response.output_text:
            raise RuntimeError(f"No complete text answer (status: {response.status}).")
        return response.output_text


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("question")
    parser.add_argument("--hosted", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(ask(args.question, hosted=args.hosted))

python -m examples.model_call "What is the return policy?"

Expect Fixture response: use a source document to verify the answer.

docs.title: How a hosted call works
docs.text:
The hosted branch sends the question and a short instruction to a deployment. During inference the model generates tokens based on its input. The API returns a response object with a status and output items. The SDK assembles text from the response as output_text. The example checks for a completed response so an incomplete result does not pass as a finished answer.

Optional hosted call

You need an Azure subscription, a supported Azure OpenAI model deployment, an endpoint, and a permitted API key. Confirm region and quota before sending requests, which may incur usage charges. Install the SDK with python -m pip install "openai>=2,<3". Set AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT to your resource URL, AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT to your deployment name, and AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY through your environment. Then run python -m examples.model_call "What is the return policy?" --hosted. Expect a short answer whose wording can vary. Give the model a synthetic question so the exercise does not transmit private policy text. Azure OpenAI Responses API

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: Remove AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT and run the hosted path. A missing setting causes a local KeyError before the model request. With a configured deployment, an upstream error can identify an invalid credential, unknown deployment, or exhausted rate limit. Record the status and provider request ID when available.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Set a request deadline and handle transient failures under that deadline. Keep secrets separate from logs and source code. Consider Microsoft Entra authentication for deployed workloads. Review your data handling requirements before sending document content to an inference service.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can swap the model behind one application function and distinguish local configuration from upstream behavior. Next: Expose a typed API

Foundry endpoints

docs.title: Build a Python CLI
docs.text:
Build a command-line interface for Document Assistant. You will give it a question, check the input, and test its behavior before adding a model.

Core · 45 minutes · Prerequisites Python 3.11 or later and a terminal.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An application needs a clear boundary between what a user enters and what the program does with it. Start with the smallest version of that boundary. A function receives a string, checks it, and returns a value or raises an error.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
Save the following as examples/cli.py or use the copy in the handbook source.

"""Ask the fixture a question from your terminal."""

import argparse


def answer(question: str) -> str:
    question = question.strip()
    if not question:
        raise ValueError("Enter a question.")
    return f"You asked: {question}"


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("question")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        print(answer(args.question))
    except ValueError as error:
        parser.error(str(error))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run the module from the project root. Python's -m flag locates and runs the module by its dotted name.

python -m examples.cli "How many days do I have to return an unopened headset?"

Expect You asked: How many days do I have to return an unopened headset?.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: argparse converts shell arguments into Python values. The annotation question: str describes what the function expects. The function still checks that the string contains something after trimming whitespace. The __main__ guard lets a test import the function without reading terminal arguments.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Try a whitespace-only question. Expect Enter a question. and a nonzero exit code. Read $LASTEXITCODE in PowerShell or $? in Bash immediately afterward. The shell can use that status to decide whether the next step should run.

Add a direct check for normalization. This exercise imports only the application function.

python -c "from examples.cli import answer; assert answer('  headset  ') == 'You asked: headset'"

A successful assertion prints nothing. Temporarily remove strip() and rerun it. The resulting AssertionError tells you the function's output changed even though the CLI still starts.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Keep validation close to application entry points. Give users actionable messages for invalid input. Treat unexpected exceptions as failures and log them with enough context to diagnose the operation. A small pure function remains easy to test after the terminal entry point becomes HTTP.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You built and tested the input boundary. Next: From your shell to an HTTP request

Python argparse

docs.title: Expose a typed API
docs.text:
Expose Document Assistant as a JSON API. The request schema gives callers a predictable interface and catches invalid input before it reaches the model.

Core · 60 minutes · Prerequisites Make a model call and the API dependencies below.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A CLI works for one terminal. A web client or automation needs an address, an HTTP method, and a defined request and response. FastAPI routes requests to functions. Pydantic checks the shape and constraints of data at the boundary.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
Install the API dependencies with python -m pip install -r requirements-examples.txt in your environment.

"""A Document Assistant HTTP endpoint with a deterministic model."""

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, StringConstraints

from examples.model_call import ask

app = FastAPI(title="Document Assistant")


class Question(BaseModel):
    text: Annotated[str, StringConstraints(
        strip_whitespace=True, min_length=1, max_length=500
    )]


class Answer(BaseModel):
    answer: str


@app.post("/answers")
def create_answer(question: Question) -> Answer:
    return Answer(answer=ask(question.text))

Start the tutorial server from the root.

python -m uvicorn examples.api:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001

Open http://127.0.0.1:8001/docs. Expand POST /answers, choose Try it out, and send the following body.

{"text":"What is the return policy?"}

Expect HTTP 200 and {"answer":"Fixture response: use a source document to verify the answer."}.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Uvicorn passes an HTTP request to the ASGI application. FastAPI parses the JSON body and builds a Question. The model strips whitespace and applies a length bound. FastAPI calls the route and serializes the returned Answer. The same type definitions contribute to the OpenAPI description that powers the browser UI.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Submit {"text":" "}. Expect HTTP 422 and a validation error pointing to body.text. Send a request with the wrong method and compare the 405 response. A client test can inspect both responses without binding a port.

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from examples.api import app

with TestClient(app) as client:
    response = client.post("/answers", json={"text": "   "})
    assert response.status_code == 422

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Use dependency injection for a model client and caller identity. Use middleware for concerns such as request IDs and timing. A synchronous route is appropriate for this fixture. An async route can wait for an async network client while the server handles other requests. Keep model credentials and internal exceptions out of API responses.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You exposed a typed HTTP interface and verified its validation boundary. Next: Stream an answer

FastAPI request bodies, FastAPI testing

docs.title: Keep state and enforce ownership
docs.text:
Design persistence and authorization for conversation history and uploaded documents. The design will support retrieval across multiple users.

Supporting · 85 minutes · Prerequisites Expose a typed API and basic familiarity with SQL.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Conversations disappear after a restart, and a document ID alone says nothing about who can read it. Store durable state and derive access from an authenticated caller.

docs.title: Design the data boundary
docs.text:
Use PostgreSQL for conversations, turns, document metadata, and access records. Use object storage for uploaded file bytes. PostgreSQL can update related rows in a transaction. Blob Storage handles file bytes independently. Use a generated object key and keep the original filename as display metadata.

Authentication establishes the caller's identity. Authorization checks whether that identity can act on a record. Resolve the caller from a validated token and apply the ownership condition in the same query that reads records. This PostgreSQL excerpt assumes that documents has id, owner_id, object_key, and status columns.

PREPARE owned_document (uuid, uuid) AS
SELECT id, object_key, status
FROM documents
WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;

Bind both values as parameters. The second comes from the trusted caller context. Index the columns used by common queries, for example (owner_id, created_at) for listing an owner's documents. A connection pool reuses connections, so bound pool size when you add API replicas.

docs.title: Trace an upload
docs.text: Create a pending document record. Store bytes under its generated key. Record successful upload and schedule indexing. A database transaction cannot roll back a completed object write. If updating the database fails, a cleanup task or retry can reconcile the pending record and its object key. Use migrations to evolve the schema and record which changes each environment has applied.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: Assume Alice uploads document A. Try Alice's token with A, Bob's token with A, and no token. Expect Alice to find A, Bob to receive the same response as an unknown ID, and the unauthenticated caller to receive 401. If Bob sees A, inspect the dependency that resolves identity and the actual SQL predicate. A valid token alone cannot enforce ownership.

docs.title: Engineering decisions
docs.text: PostgreSQL fits when conversations, documents, and permissions have relationships and need transactions. A document database can fit independent JSON aggregates when you know how they will be partitioned and read. In Azure, validate Entra issuer, audience, expiry, signature and required scopes. An application identity used to access storage serves a different purpose from the token sent by an end user.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You defined the ownership boundary that retrieval will enforce. Next: Budget tokens and build prompts

PostgreSQL transactions, PostgreSQL prepared statements, Microsoft Entra access tokens

docs.title: Stream an answer
docs.text:
Deliver pieces of an answer as they become available. Learn what changes when a response can fail after the HTTP headers have been sent.

Core · 65 minutes · Prerequisites Expose a typed API.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An answer can take several seconds. Waiting for the full body makes the interface feel idle. Server-Sent Events, or SSE, use a text response with named events separated by blank lines. A client can show deltas as they arrive.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
"""Send incremental text and a terminal event using SSE."""

import asyncio
import json
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

from examples.api import Question

app = FastAPI(title="Document Assistant streaming fixture")


def event(name: str, data: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    return f"event: {name}\ndata: {json.dumps(data)}\n\n"


async def answer_events(question: Question) -> AsyncIterator[str]:
    yield event("delta", {"text": "You asked: "})
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    yield event("delta", {"text": question.text})
    yield event("done", {})


@app.post("/answers/stream")
async def stream_answer(question: Question) -> StreamingResponse:
    return StreamingResponse(
        answer_events(question), media_type="text/event-stream"
    )

Start this example on port 8002 so it can run beside the previous one. In a second terminal, use the Python HTTP client to send a POST and print the received events. The with block closes the response on exit.

python -m uvicorn examples.streaming:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8002

import httpx

with httpx.stream(
    "POST", "http://127.0.0.1:8002/answers/stream",
    json={"text": "headset returns"},
) as response:
    response.raise_for_status()
    for line in response.iter_lines():
        print(line)

Expect two delta events and one done event. The short sleep stands in for waiting on a network call. While it awaits, the event loop can work on another request.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Send blank input. Expect 422 before the stream starts. Then remove the done event temporarily. The connection still ends cleanly at the HTTP level. The client should treat the answer as incomplete because it never received the application-level completion signal.

For a real provider stream, map provider errors to a terminal error event after streaming starts, and release its connection when the client disconnects. Browser clients can consume a POST stream with fetch. The built-in EventSource API opens a GET stream.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Track time to first token separately from total duration. Set deadlines for opening and reading the upstream stream. A bounded retry can help before any data is sent, subject to cost and request semantics. Retrying after a visible delta can duplicate or contradict text. Watch for reverse proxy buffering and match timeouts to the stream's idle behavior. Use a durable job for long-lived ingestion work that must survive API restarts.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can distinguish a successful HTTP connection from a complete streamed answer. Next: Keep state and enforce ownership

FastAPI streaming responses, Python asyncio

docs.title: Budget tokens and build prompts
docs.text:
Build the input a model actually sees. You will keep the current question, reserve room for output, and select which conversation turns fit.

Core · 65 minutes · Prerequisites Make a model call.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Documents and long conversations can exceed a model's context window. Even when everything fits, extra material can add cost, delay the response, and distract from relevant evidence.

docs.title: Understand the input
docs.text:
A tokenizer maps text to pieces called tokens. A token might be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or a piece of a string used in code. During generation a transformer uses attention to combine information from the available token positions and predicts the next token. An output can sound confident because it follows a likely language pattern. Its wording alone gives no proof that a claim is true.

Budget instructions, the latest user message, history, retrieved passages, and output. With a budget of 4,000 tokens, reserve 600 for output and 900 for fixed instructions and the question. The remaining 2,500 can be allocated to history and evidence. Count provider-specific overhead too.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
The exercise uses characters as a simple, deterministic stand-in. A hosted model needs the tokenizer or count facility appropriate to its model.

"""Fit complete recent turns inside a character budget for a local exercise."""


def select_history(turns: list[str], budget: int) -> list[str]:
    if budget < 0:
        raise ValueError("The fixed prompt already exceeds the budget.")
    selected = []
    for turn in reversed(turns):
        turn_cost = len(turn) + 1  # Include a newline separator.
        if turn_cost > budget:
            break
        selected.append(turn)
        budget -= turn_cost
    return list(reversed(selected))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(select_history(["User: hello", "User: return an unopened headset"], 35))

Run python -m examples.context. Expect ['User: return an unopened headset']. The latest complete turn fits. Adding the older turn would exceed the remaining budget.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Try a budget of 5. Expect no history. A negative budget signals that the fixed prompt itself exceeds the limit. Reduce the fixed prompt or reject the request with an explanation. In an actual conversation keep tool calls and their results together when selecting turns.

Test two instructions with the same input. First ask for a policy answer. Then specify the desired format and say to abstain if the supplied documents do not support it. Compare the outputs on both a supported question and a missing-evidence question. Use labeled samples when deciding which instruction works better.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Version instructions, output budget, and history selection together. Retain the current user question and constrain the number and length of chunks. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data. Separating it from instructions helps the model interpret it, while tool authorization still belongs in application code.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can account for context, output budget, and the role of prompts in a repeatable experiment. Next: Validate model output and tool calls

OpenAI Cookbook tokenizer example

docs.title: Choose a model and serving strategy
docs.text:
Pick an inference strategy using measurements from the kind of questions Document Assistant actually receives.

Core · 75 minutes · Prerequisites Budget tokens and build prompts and Validate model output and tool calls.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A stronger model can improve a difficult answer while making an ordinary request slower or more expensive. A large context window can make a design possible without making it efficient. Set acceptance criteria before choosing a deployment.

docs.title: Understand serving
docs.text:
Inference is model execution to produce a prediction or response. Request time includes queueing, processing the input, generating output, and network transfers. An inference server can batch requests to improve throughput, while waiting for a batch can increase latency for one user. Streaming exposes the first output sooner. It does not reduce all the work the server performs.

Managed inference gives you an endpoint and leaves much of the serving operation to the provider. Self-hosted inference can give you more control over hardware, data placement, and runtime tuning. It also makes capacity planning, patches, model licensing and operational coverage your responsibility.

docs.title: Work a model selection example
docs.text:
The table is synthetic. Both candidates answered the same 50 questions with the same retrieval pipeline. A grounded answer is supported by the retrieved evidence.

Candidate Grounded answers p95 response time Cost per 1,000 questions A 45/50 1.8 s $1.40 B 48/50 3.1 s $4.80

Require at least 90% grounded answers, p95 under 2.5 seconds, and cost under $3. Candidate A meets these thresholds. Before adopting it, inspect which five questions it missed. Aggregate quality can hide a failure on a critical policy.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Candidate A fails questions about a policy version absent from the index. Compare the retrieved chunks to the labeled source before changing the model. Expect retrieval recall to fail for the missing version. Add the correct document, reindex, and repeat the same comparison.

Use prompting for an improved instruction or format. Add retrieval when current external facts or citations matter. Consider fine-tuning for a durable behavior change when prompt and data improvements have plateaued and you have representative training and evaluation examples.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Version the selected deployment, prompts, and evaluator together. Set quotas and deadlines. Watch rate-limit responses and the effect of retries on throughput and cost. Test the fallback's behavior on the same questions before routing real requests to it.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You selected a model under explicit quality, latency, and cost constraints. Next: Ingest documents and build chunks

Foundry model catalog, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints

docs.title: Validate model output and tool calls
docs.text:
Use Pydantic to validate a model-suggested search. The model proposes arguments, and your code decides whether to execute the tool.

Core · 70 minutes · Prerequisites Expose a typed API and the dependencies in requirements-examples.txt.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A caller expects a search query and a small result limit. The model might return prose, a wrong type, or a plausible-looking request outside the caller's permissions.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
"""Validate output at the boundary between a model and application code."""

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, ValidationError


class SearchDocuments(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)

    query: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=500)
    limit: int = Field(ge=1, le=5)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    valid = SearchDocuments.model_validate_json('{"query":"headset","limit":2}')
    print(valid.model_dump_json())
    try:
        SearchDocuments.model_validate_json('{"query":"headset","limit":"2"}')
    except ValidationError as error:
        print("Rejected:", error.errors()[0]["loc"][0])

Run python -m examples.structured. Expect {"query":"headset","limit":2} followed by Rejected: limit. Strict validation catches an incoming string where code expects an integer. Forbidding extras helps expose unexpected fields before a developer mistakes them for supported arguments.

docs.title: How it fits
docs.text:
With structured outputs, a supported provider can constrain generated data to a JSON Schema. Use that feature when downstream code needs a stable structure. With function calling, the response includes a proposed tool name and arguments. Dispatch only registered tools, validate arguments locally, and attach the actual caller identity to the call.

Document Assistant sends a typed search definition, receives a call such as search_documents, validates its arguments, and runs an ownership-filtered search. It can pass the tool result back to the model alongside the corresponding call ID. The tool's output is also data and can contain untrusted text.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: Replace the result limit with 50, add an owner_id property, or send malformed JSON. Check what error each input produces. For the first two, expect a range error and an extra-field error. A valid limit and query can still yield no results. Give that case a distinct outcome.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Handle refusals and truncated responses separately from schema failures. A provider may support a subset of JSON Schema. Use the versioned API reference for the chosen deployment and exercise its real outputs with an integration test. Give tools clear descriptions, bounded inputs, and narrowly scoped permissions.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You validated model output and separated argument validation from execution authority. Next: Choose a model and serving strategy

Pydantic strict mode, Foundry structured outputs

docs.title: Cite sources and evaluate RAG
docs.text:
Make answers verifiable and measure whether the retriever finds known evidence. Separate a ranking failure from a generation or citation failure.

Core · 95 minutes · Prerequisites Search by keyword and meaning.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An answer can be wrong because the right chunk was missing or because the model ignored it. Evaluating final text alone makes it hard to tell where to fix the application.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
This fixture returns the leading authorized passage as the answer. Its narrow behavior makes retrieval and citations easy to inspect without a model.

"""Evaluate retrieval and citation behavior on a tiny labeled fixture."""

from examples.retrieval import retrieve


def cited_answer(query: str, owner: str) -> tuple[str, list[str]]:
    matches = retrieve(query, owner, limit=1)
    if not matches:
        return "No supporting evidence was found.", []
    source = matches[0]
    return source.text, [source.id]


def main() -> None:
    cases = [
        ("headset returns", "training", "returns-v1#1"),
        ("standard shipping", "training", "shipping-v1#1"),
        ("headset returns", "partner", "partner-v1#1"),
    ]
    hits = sum(
        expected in {chunk.id for chunk in retrieve(query, owner, limit=1)}
        for query, owner, expected in cases
    )
    print(f"Recall@1: {hits / len(cases):.2f} ({hits}/{len(cases)})")
    for query in ("headset returns", "international warranty"):
        answer, citations = cited_answer(query, "training")
        print(answer, citations)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Run python -m examples.evaluation. Expect these results.

Recall@1: 1.00 (3/3)
Unopened headset returns are accepted within 30 days. ['returns-v1#1']
No supporting evidence was found. []

docs.title: Interpret the result
docs.text:
For each test question, recall at k is the fraction of its labeled relevant chunks found in the first k retrieval results. The dataset here has one relevant chunk per question. The printed number averages recall over three labeled queries.

For a generated answer, measure whether its factual claims are supported. Verify citation IDs belong to the supplied authorized candidates and review whether those passages support the claims they are attached to. An existing citation can still be the wrong source. Track abstention on unanswerable questions separately.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Add the following item to cases and rerun.

("refund headphones", "training", "returns-v1#1"),

The score drops to 0.75 (3/4). Inspect the query terms and evidence to see why. Repeat with synonyms or a hybrid implementation. Include documents with similar wording and different policy dates so the benchmark catches plausible wrong answers.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Save the question, allowed scope, expected evidence and dataset version together. Measure recall, citation validity, and grounded answers by slice. Use representative held-out questions before release and privacy-reviewed samples afterward. Pair human reviews with automated checks for important or ambiguous cases.

docs.text:
You diagnosed one retrieval failure and defined separate quality checks for generation. Next: Build a deterministic tool workflow

Microsoft Foundry RAG evaluators

docs.title: Ingest documents and build chunks
docs.text:
Turn documents into searchable records with stable citation IDs. Start with paragraphs and work through how a larger ingestion pipeline would parse and embed them.

Core · 75 minutes · Prerequisites Keep state and enforce ownership.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Passing each whole file to the model wastes context. Searching a file needs smaller units of evidence that still make sense when read independently and can be traced back to the original.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
A chunk is a portion of source text that can be retrieved on its own. For short synthetic documents, treat each paragraph as a chunk.

"""Turn paragraph-shaped synthetic policies into addressable chunks."""

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Chunk:
    id: str
    owner: str
    text: str


def chunk_document(document_id: str, owner: str, text: str) -> list[Chunk]:
    paragraphs = [part.strip() for part in text.split("\n\n") if part.strip()]
    return [
        Chunk(f"{document_id}#{position}", owner, paragraph)
        for position, paragraph in enumerate(paragraphs, start=1)
    ]


DOCUMENTS = chunk_document(
    "returns-v1", "training", "Unopened headset returns are accepted within 30 days."
    "\n\nSend a receipt with the unopened item.",
) + chunk_document(
    "shipping-v1", "training", "Standard shipping takes five business days."
) + chunk_document(
    "partner-v1", "partner", "Unopened headset returns are accepted within 90 days."
)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for chunk in DOCUMENTS[:2]:
        print(f"{chunk.id}: {chunk.text}")

Run python -m examples.ingestion. Expect the following IDs and text.

returns-v1#1: Unopened headset returns are accepted within 30 days.
returns-v1#2: Send a receipt with the unopened item.

docs.title: How chunking works
docs.text:
A parser turns bytes into text and source locations. A chunker chooses boundaries. An embedding model maps each chunk to a vector that a retrieval engine can compare with query vectors. Store the chunk ID, document version, owner, source location and embedding model alongside the text and vector. Stable IDs make citations testable and help with retries.

For Markdown, a heading plus paragraphs can preserve section meaning. For PDFs with selectable text, use page numbers and inspect reading order. Scanned PDFs typically need optical character recognition. A parser can succeed while producing unusable text, so verify text length and review sample pages before indexing.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: Move the return deadline into its own paragraph. Retrieve on “headset returns” in the next lesson and inspect whether the returned paragraph still includes the number. If it does not, try a section-based chunk or a small overlap. Overlap preserves context at a boundary and can increase duplicates, storage and cost.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Set file size and parser limits. Record extraction and indexing status separately. Avoid indexing a partial upload. Use a document revision and deterministic chunk IDs so a retried job overwrites its own output. Track embedding model changes and rebuild the index when you change embedding space.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You created stable chunks and understand how parser and chunk decisions affect retrieval. Next: Search by keyword and meaning

pypdf text extraction, Foundry embeddings

docs.title: Search by keyword and meaning
docs.text:
Build the first search baseline and compare it with vector and hybrid retrieval. Document permissions affect the candidate set before ranking begins.

Core · 85 minutes · Prerequisites Ingest documents and build chunks.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An exact match can find a product code, yet users often describe the same item with a synonym. A semantic search can help with synonyms. You still need a permission boundary shared by every retrieval strategy.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
The fixture scores chunks by the number of query terms they share. Ownership is checked before a chunk receives a score.

"""Rank an authorized set of chunks by shared keywords."""

import re

from examples.ingestion import DOCUMENTS, Chunk

STOP_WORDS = {"a", "an", "are", "do", "does", "how", "i", "the", "to", "within"}


def words(text: str) -> set[str]:
    return set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())) - STOP_WORDS


def retrieve(query: str, owner: str, limit: int = 3) -> list[Chunk]:
    query_words = words(query)
    scores = [
        (len(query_words & words(chunk.text)), chunk)
        for chunk in DOCUMENTS
        if chunk.owner == owner
    ]
    scores.sort(key=lambda pair: (-pair[0], pair[1].id))
    return [chunk for score, chunk in scores if score > 0][:limit]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for chunk in retrieve("headset returns", "training"):
        print(chunk.id)

Run python -m examples.retrieval. Expect returns-v1#1 only. The partner chunk contains the same search terms and belongs to a different owner.

docs.title: Add vector search
docs.text:
An embedding is a vector of numbers. Compare query and document vectors produced by the same model and configuration. Cosine distance measures their direction relative to one another. Lower distance means a closer match. The PostgreSQL excerpt assumes pgvector is installed, owner_id is a UUID, and all stored vectors use the query's dimensions.

PREPARE vector_search (uuid, vector) AS
SELECT id, text, embedding <=> $2 AS distance
FROM chunks
WHERE owner_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 5;

Connect the owner parameter to authenticated identity. Start with exact search for a small corpus. Measure recall and latency before adopting an approximate index such as HNSW. Selective filters can leave approximate search with too few matches, so inspect filtered recall on a representative dataset.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text:
Search for “refund headphones”. Expect the keyword fixture to return no results. Add this query to the labeled dataset and compare it with semantic retrieval in a real system. A synonym can be semantically close without being an exact match.

A hybrid ranker combines keyword and vector candidates. Reciprocal rank fusion adds values such as 1 / (60 + rank) from each ranked list. It uses positions and avoids assuming the raw keyword and vector scores share a scale. Reranking can apply a stronger relevance scorer to a small pool at the cost of an extra inference step.

The following exercise gives the query and chunks illustrative vectors so you can examine rank fusion without a hosted model.

"""Combine keyword results with a tiny fixed-vector search."""

from collections import defaultdict
from math import hypot

from examples.ingestion import DOCUMENTS, Chunk
from examples.retrieval import retrieve

# Two illustrative axes: how much a chunk is about returns and about shipping.
VECTORS = {
    "returns-v1#1": (1.0, 0.0),
    "returns-v1#2": (0.7, 0.2),
    "shipping-v1#1": (0.0, 1.0),
    "partner-v1#1": (1.0, 0.0),
}


def cosine(left: tuple[float, float], right: tuple[float, float]) -> float:
    dot = left[0] * right[0] + left[1] * right[1]
    return dot / (hypot(*left) * hypot(*right))


def hybrid_search(
    query: str, query_vector: tuple[float, float], owner: str
) -> list[Chunk]:
    candidates = [chunk for chunk in DOCUMENTS if chunk.owner == owner]
    semantic = sorted(
        candidates, key=lambda chunk: -cosine(query_vector, VECTORS[chunk.id])
    )[:2]
    scores: dict[str, float] = defaultdict(float)
    for ranking in (retrieve(query, owner, limit=2), semantic):
        for rank, chunk in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[chunk.id] += 1 / (60 + rank)
    return sorted(
        (chunk for chunk in candidates if chunk.id in scores),
        key=lambda chunk: (-scores[chunk.id], chunk.id),
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = hybrid_search("refund headphones", (1.0, 0.1), "training")
    print([chunk.id for chunk in result])

Run python -m examples.hybrid. Expect ['returns-v1#1', 'returns-v1#2']. Change the query vector to (0.1, 1.0) and rerun. Shipping should rank first even though the text is still “refund headphones”. In a real system the same embedding model generates both document and query vectors, so this mismatch would be a test for a configuration or data-flow error.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Apply tenant and document permissions to each retriever. Keep them in force when resolving a citation. PostgreSQL and pgvector share existing metadata and operational tooling. Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) is an optional comparison when managed indexing or independent search scaling solves a measured need.

docs.text:

docs.title: Bound agent runs and approve writes
docs.text:
Run a small agent loop, pause before a write, and handle the same approval twice. The model proposes. Application code owns the decision and write.

Core · 90 minutes · Prerequisites Build a deterministic tool workflow.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A model can misunderstand the user's request or follow misleading text in a document. A note-saving action needs a clear permission boundary and a way for the user to confirm exactly what will be saved.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
This fixture stores one immutable proposal per run, compares the verified actor with the proposal owner, then records the first decision. The repeat returns the existing decision.

"""Model the state transitions for a single in-memory note proposal."""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Literal


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Proposal:
    run_id: str
    owner: str
    text: str


@dataclass
class NoteStore:
    proposals: dict[str, Proposal] = field(default_factory=dict)
    decisions: dict[str, Literal["approved", "rejected"]] = field(default_factory=dict)
    notes: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def propose(self, proposal: Proposal) -> None:
        if proposal.run_id in self.proposals:
            raise ValueError("Run already has a proposal.")
        if not proposal.text.strip() or len(proposal.text) > 500:
            raise ValueError("A note must have 1 to 500 characters.")
        self.proposals[proposal.run_id] = proposal

    def decide(self, run_id: str, actor: str, *, approved: bool) -> str:
        proposal = self.proposals[run_id]
        if actor != proposal.owner:
            raise PermissionError("Only the owner can decide.")
        if run_id not in self.decisions:
            if approved:
                self.notes[run_id] = proposal.text
                self.decisions[run_id] = "approved"
            else:
                self.decisions[run_id] = "rejected"
        return self.decisions[run_id]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    store = NoteStore()
    store.propose(Proposal("run-1", "training", "Review the returns policy."))
    print(f"Before approval: {len(store.notes)} notes")
    print(store.decide("run-1", "training", approved=True))
    store.decide("run-1", "training", approved=True)
    print(f"After repeating approval: {len(store.notes)} note")

Run python -m examples.approvals. Expect zero notes before approval, approved, and one note after repeating approval. In this in-memory example each dictionary disappears when the process exits.

docs.title: Add a bounded loop
docs.text:
Run python -m examples.agent. The scripted model first selects search, observes an authorized citation ID, then proposes a note. Expect awaiting_approval and Saved notes: 0. The loop can also finish, reject a bad tool or argument, or reach its three-step limit. Review agent evaluation for the implementation.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Running
    Running --> AwaitingApproval : Valid note proposal
    Running --> Finished : Done or budget reached
    AwaitingApproval --> Approved : Owner approves
    AwaitingApproval --> Rejected : Owner rejects or proposal expires

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: Call decide as another owner and expect PermissionError. Confirm the note count stays zero. Start a fresh run, reject it, and then retry with approval. Expect the first decision, rejected, and zero notes.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Persist the run and proposed arguments. Bind approval to the authenticated actor, run and exact proposal. Show the action before the decision and expire old proposals. Use a transaction and unique action identifier to make the approval and write safe under retries and racing requests. Set tool, time and token budgets. Treat document text as untrusted and keep authorization in the tools and storage queries.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You separated model proposals, human decisions, and side effects. Next: Evaluate and orchestrate agents

LangGraph interrupts

docs.title: Evaluate and orchestrate agents
docs.text:
Evaluate an agent by the actions it took and the state it left behind. See where a graph and persistent checkpoints add value.

Core · 85 minutes · Prerequisites Bound agent runs and approve writes.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An answer like “Done” can conceal a failed tool call or an unauthorized write. Inspect the trajectory, meaning the sequence of actions, results, and decisions.

docs.title: Run and debug a scripted agent
docs.text:
The callback supplies model-like tool proposals. Keeping it scripted makes the sequence predictable while you test the application loop.

"""Use scripted model proposals to exercise a bounded tool loop."""

from collections.abc import Callable

from examples.approvals import NoteStore, Proposal
from examples.retrieval import retrieve

ChooseTool = Callable[[list[str]], tuple[str, str]]


def run(
    run_id: str, owner: str, choose_tool: ChooseTool, store: NoteStore
) -> str:
    observations: list[str] = []
    for _ in range(3):
        tool, argument = choose_tool(observations.copy())
        if tool == "finish":
            return "finished"
        if not argument.strip() or len(argument) > 500:
            return "invalid_arguments"
        if tool == "search_documents":
            matches = retrieve(argument, owner, limit=2)
            observations.extend(chunk.id for chunk in matches)
        elif tool == "propose_note":
            store.propose(Proposal(run_id, owner, argument))
            return "awaiting_approval"
        else:
            return "unknown_tool"
    return "step_limit"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    def choose_tool(observations: list[str]) -> tuple[str, str]:
        if observations:
            return "propose_note", f"Review {observations[0]}."
        return "search_documents", "headset returns"

    store = NoteStore()
    print(run("run-1", "training", choose_tool, store))
    print(f"Saved notes: {len(store.notes)}")

Run python -m examples.agent. Expect a pause with zero saved notes. Replace the callback with one that always selects search_documents. Expect step_limit after three calls. Try an unknown tool and verify the loop exits without a write.

docs.title: Compare expected trajectories
docs.text:
Case Expected path What to inspect Find a policy Search → finish Authorized citation IDs and time spent Prepare a note Search → propose → pause Exact note proposal and zero saved notes Rejected proposal Pause → reject No duplicate or delayed write Misleading source text Search → bounded decision Tool allowlist and unchanged privileges

Memory is information carried forward. Keep short-lived observations and persisted run state separate from long-term user preferences. Review what deserves to be retained and enforce tenant scoping and retention for both.

docs.title: Optional LangGraph exercise
docs.text:
Map search, propose, and decision to graph nodes. Use a checkpointer to save state, a stable thread ID scoped to the caller, and interrupt() to pause with a proposal. Resume with Command(resume=decision) after the application validates the actor. The node executes from its beginning when resumed, so put the durable write after the decision and make it idempotent. LangGraph interrupts

The following optional fixture pauses a single node and then resumes it. Install langgraph>=1,<2 in the tutorial environment and save the example as graph_pause.py.

from typing import TypedDict

from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph
from langgraph.types import Command, interrupt


class State(TypedDict, total=False):
    note: str
    outcome: str


def review(state: State) -> dict[str, str]:
    approved = interrupt({"proposed_note": state["note"]})
    return {"outcome": "approved" if approved is True else "rejected"}


builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("review", review)
builder.add_edge(START, "review")
builder.add_edge("review", END)
graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "training-run-1"}}
paused = graph.invoke({"note": "Review the returns policy."}, config)
assert "__interrupt__" in paused
resumed = graph.invoke(Command(resume=False), config)
print(resumed["outcome"])

Run python graph_pause.py and expect rejected. This uses an in-memory checkpoint, so the two invocations run in the same process. Change the thread ID for the resume call to see why the approval request must identify the right run.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Use one agent or a deterministic graph while it meets the goal. Consider specialized agents for genuinely independent subtasks with explicit handoffs. Measure extra model calls, lost context, and coordination failure before expanding. Trace tool names and outcomes, approval waits, budgets, and resume behavior without recording private arguments by default.

docs.text:

docs.title: Build a deterministic tool workflow
docs.text:
Give Document Assistant two explicit actions. You will learn what makes a workflow deterministic before letting a model choose a tool.

Core · 65 minutes · Prerequisites Validate model output and tool calls and Search by keyword and meaning.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Answering a question is different from performing an operation. The application needs to know which capabilities it can call and which ones may change state.

docs.title: Your first working example
docs.text:
A workflow encodes steps and decisions in application code. This example chooses an action from an explicit input. Both actions are read-only because previewing a note returns text to the user without saving it.

"""Route a tool request with an explicit user-selected action."""

from typing import Literal

from examples.retrieval import retrieve


def run(
    action: Literal["search", "preview_note"], question: str, owner: str
) -> list[str]:
    if action == "search":
        return [chunk.id for chunk in retrieve(question, owner)]
    if action == "preview_note":
        return [f"Draft: {question}"]
    raise ValueError("Unknown action.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(run("search", "headset returns", "training"))
    print(run("preview_note", "Review the returns policy.", "training"))

Run python -m examples.workflow. Expect ['returns-v1#1'] and ['Draft: Review the returns policy.'].

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The search dispatch uses the caller scope. The preview builds a draft in memory. A real HTTP route would validate the action and derive the owner from the authenticated session.

An agent lets a model choose the next action based on the goal and results so far. Document Assistant can already answer policy questions with a fixed retrieve-then-answer workflow. Agentic choice is useful when the user describes a goal with unclear steps, such as locating relevant policy evidence and preparing a note for review.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: Call run("delete", "headset", "training") from Python. Expect ValueError: Unknown action.. Observe that a type hint helps a type checker while the explicit runtime guard handles unexpected data. Try a valid search as partner and verify the returned chunk belongs to that owner.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Use operations with explicit, narrow inputs. A search tool should expose a query and limit and let application code decide the database scope. Give tool calls separate time budgets. Keep deterministic flows where the steps are known so you can measure and test them directly.

docs.title: Map the application to Azure
docs.text:
Choose Azure services for the running example and trace how the user and the workload each establish identity.

Supporting · 70 minutes · Prerequisites Package the API with Docker and Keep state and enforce ownership.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A hosted Document Assistant needs a public request entry point, secure connections to its dependencies, and a way for operators to observe failures. The service choices should match the workload.

docs.title: Sketch the topology
docs.text:
This diagram is an architecture walkthrough. Exact subnet, access and region choices depend on the environment.

flowchart LR
    U["User with Entra access token"] -->|HTTPS| A["Container Apps API"]
    A --> P["PostgreSQL Flexible Server + pgvector"]
    A --> B["Blob Storage"]
    A --> F["Microsoft Foundry model deployment"]
    A --> M["Azure Monitor and Application Insights"]
    R["Container Registry"] -->|image pull| A
Component Responsibility Container Apps Runs the HTTP container and manages ingress and revisions PostgreSQL Flexible Server Holds conversations, permissions, jobs and vector data Blob Storage Holds uploaded bytes with anonymous access disabled Microsoft Foundry Hosts the selected chat and embedding deployments Azure Monitor and Application Insights Collects application and platform telemetry

A subscription groups billing and access. A resource group groups resources for management and lifecycle. A region affects latency, data location, quota and service availability. Azure operates the managed platform. You still own data access, app settings, permission scopes and operational response.

docs.title: Trace one authenticated request
docs.text:
The API validates the end user's token and applies document access rules. The Container App can use managed identity to acquire a service token. Grant that identity the minimum data role at each service scope. For PostgreSQL with Entra authentication, map the identity to a database role and grant SQL permissions. For Blob, a container-scoped data role limits the workload's reach. Key Vault can hold a secret for an integration that still needs one.

Place PostgreSQL on private networking when the application can reach its private address. Check DNS and routes before debugging credentials. A 403 from Blob indicates that a request reached the service. Check the identity, data role, destination, and storage network rules.

docs.title: Compare the options
docs.text:
App Service can fit a conventional web app. Functions can fit event handlers with an appropriate execution and scaling model. Container Apps fits a web container and a separate worker without operating a Kubernetes cluster. AKS gives teams more orchestration control along with cluster responsibility. A virtual machine fits requirements for OS-level control and adds patching and host management.

Optional Kubernetes vocabulary

A pod is the smallest deployable workload unit. A Deployment rolls out replicas of pods and replaces them when needed. A Service gives clients a stable way to reach those replicas. A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler can adjust replica count using configured metrics. In AKS, platform setup and workload operations still need explicit owners. Kubernetes objects

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text:
Assume the API identity receives a Blob data permission error after deployment. Show where you would check the account, container, token audience, role assignment scope, and which runtime identity requested the token. Confirm that a different identity without a data role gets denied. Treat role propagation and network restrictions as separate evidence to inspect.

A real deployment needs subscription access, resource and role assignment permissions, model capacity and quota, and a budget. Check current regional availability and treat logs, database capacity and inference as separate cost drivers.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can explain the service boundaries, network path, and two kinds of identity. Next: Describe infrastructure with Terraform
