docs.title: Package the API with Docker
docs.text:
Read a Dockerfile for the API you already built. Follow the connection from a host port to Uvicorn inside the container.

Supporting · 50 minutes · Prerequisites Expose a typed API.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: An API can depend on a developer's Python version, packages, and files. An image describes the application filesystem and startup command. A container is a process started from that image with isolation and runtime settings.

docs.title: Walk through a Dockerfile
docs.text:
This teaching example packages the fixture API from the project root. Read each line before considering a build.

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements-examples.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements-examples.txt
COPY examples/ ./examples/
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "-m", "uvicorn", "examples.api:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

The dependency layer can be reused when source files change. COPY reads files from the build context. Keep credentials and generated site files out of that context in a real project. An image can be pushed to a registry and identified by a digest of its content.

EXPOSE documents the intended container port. A mapping such as 127.0.0.1:8001:8000 would publish it on the host loopback address. The application listens on all container interfaces so traffic can reach it through that mapping.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text:
Imagine the image runs and logs “Uvicorn running” but the host gets connection refused. Compare the published host port with the request URL and the container port with the Uvicorn command. If Uvicorn binds only to 127.0.0.1 inside the container, it is listening on the wrong interface for published traffic.

How would the API reach a Postgres container? With Compose it would normally address the database by its service name on the shared network. A database volume keeps data across container replacements. Inside a container, localhost refers to that same container.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Pin and scan release images, run with a limited user, and pass runtime settings outside the image. A readiness check keeps traffic away until required dependencies are usable. A liveness check should detect a stuck process without turning a database outage into constant restarts.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can read a container build and reason about ports, processes, and persistence. Next: Map the application to Azure

Docker overview, Dockerfile reference

docs.title: Test, promote and roll back releases
docs.text:
Promote a tested image through environments and rehearse a rollback. Carry the same application policies and evaluation criteria into each stage.

Supporting · 60 minutes · Prerequisites Describe infrastructure with Terraform and Package the API with Docker.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A new image can pass readiness and still answer policy questions incorrectly. A release needs application checks, AI quality checks, a reproducible artifact, and a way to restore traffic.

docs.title: Read a delivery workflow
docs.text:
This GitHub Actions step excerpt assumes the repository has been checked out, Python selected, and tutorial dependencies installed inside the job.

steps:
  - name: Check the handbook
    run: python -m mkdocs build --strict
  - name: Print retrieval benchmark evidence
    run: python -m examples.evaluation

The second step prints evidence. It needs assertions or an explicit threshold gate to block a release. Add separate checks for tenant isolation and write approval. Do not rely on an average quality score to detect a security regression.

docs.title: Trace a release
docs.text:
1. On a pull request, run tests, compare evaluation results and review config changes.
  2. After merge, build an image, publish it, and record its digest with prompt, model, and dataset versions.
  3. Deploy that digest to staging. Check readiness, authentication, citations, and stream completion.
  4. Promote the identical digest to production behind an environment approval when required. Start with a small traffic share in Container Apps multiple-revision mode and compare error and quality signals.
  5. Move traffic back to the previous healthy revision when the release breaches the agreed gate. Capture the revision IDs and the reason.

GitHub's OIDC token can be exchanged for a short-lived Azure credential by a trusted deployment job. Restrict federation to the expected repository and environment claims. Give PR jobs read-only permissions, and restrict id-token: write and Azure deployment permissions to the release job.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: Revision B passes health checks. The sample question starts citing an older policy after promotion. Switch traffic back to A, then check if A can read the current schema and corpus. Expect returning traffic to recover the previous behavior only if those dependencies are compatible. A migration that dropped an old column may require a forward fix or data recovery instead.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Use additive schema changes first and remove old fields after existing revisions no longer need them. Treat model and prompt settings as part of the release. A rollback should restore compatible inputs and state as well as code. Document whether each setting is revision-scoped or shared across revisions.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can separate artifact promotion, traffic management, and data compatibility. Next: Observe quality, latency and cost

GitHub Actions OIDC in Azure, Container Apps revisions

docs.title: Describe infrastructure with Terraform
docs.text:
Read infrastructure as code and interpret a Terraform plan. Learn which changes are easy to roll back and which require a migration.

Supporting · 60 minutes · Prerequisites Map the application to Azure.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A manually configured staging environment can drift from production. Terraform records infrastructure intent in configuration and compares it with the resources tracked in its state.

docs.title: Read a configuration excerpt
docs.text:
An Azure resource group provides a small example of a resource. This excerpt assumes the AzureRM provider is declared and authenticated, and the target subscription is selected.

variable "location" {
  type = string
}

resource "azurerm_resource_group" "assistant" {
  name     = "rg-document-assistant-staging"
  location = var.location

  tags = {
    application = "document-assistant"
    environment = "staging"
  }
}

The provider translates resource and property definitions into Azure API calls. Terraform addresses this resource as azurerm_resource_group.assistant. Configuration is what you want. State maps Terraform addresses to real resources. A plan shows the candidate steps to reconcile them.

docs.title: Trace an environment change
docs.text:
Use terraform fmt -check to check formatting. In a configured workspace, terraform init prepares providers and the backend, and terraform validate checks configuration. terraform plan reads current infrastructure and proposes changes. A separate apply step changes resources. For an Azure lab, planning and applying need suitable subscription permissions and the resources created can incur charges.

Separate production and staging state and access. Remote state can be shared and locked. The AzureRM backend can store it in Azure Blob Storage. Limit who can read it because values marked sensitive can still appear there. Keep application settings in environment configuration and access secrets through a supported store such as Key Vault.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: A reviewer sees an update to tags and a replacement of the database. Identify which entry can affect customer data. For the replacement, inspect the changed property and provider explanation, then require a migration and recovery plan before applying. Determine whether an apparent creation instead comes from using the wrong state backend or environment.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Pin the provider version you validate and commit its lockfile. Review changes in the same environment and identity that will apply them. Assign one owner for each mutable property across Terraform and the release pipeline so the next apply does not undo a release.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can explain what Terraform plans, where state lives, and why a replacement deserves a separate review. Next: Test, promote and roll back releases

Terraform plan, AzureRM backend

docs.title: Scale ingestion with queues and workers
docs.text:
Move slow parsing and embedding off the request path. Design a worker that can retry without publishing duplicate or incomplete chunks.

Core · 85 minutes · Prerequisites Ingest documents and build chunks and Keep state and enforce ownership.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: If an upload request waits for every page to parse and embed, it can time out halfway through. Retrying the request may start a second copy. Separate accepting the upload from processing it.

docs.title: Walk through an ingestion pipeline
docs.text:
Store the upload and mark its version pending. Enqueue an identifier for that version. A worker claims the job for a limited lease, fetches authorized data, parses, validates and embeds it, then publishes the revision. A status endpoint reports progress. Keep the queue message small and fetch document contents through an authorized service connection.

flowchart LR
    U["Upload API"] --> B["Uploaded bytes"]
    U --> Q["Durable job"]
    Q --> W["Worker with lease"]
    B --> W
    W --> P["Write versioned chunks"]
    P --> R["Mark version searchable"]

Use a key such as (document_id, version, chunk_number). Write chunks and update publish status in a transaction. A retry can replace its own deterministic chunk IDs. Check that the worker still holds the current lease before committing so a late result cannot overwrite a newer attempt. Use exponential backoff with a retry limit and route persistent failures to a failed state or dead-letter queue.

docs.title: Choose a delivery model
docs.text:
A PostgreSQL job table is a practical starting point when job creation and metadata need one transaction. A worker can claim rows using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a short transaction and perform parsing after releasing the database lock. Azure Service Bus is an optional next step for durable message delivery and features such as dead-letter queues. If a database update and an external message must happen together, write a transactional outbox record and publish from it.

ETL transforms data before loading the target. ELT loads source data first and transforms where it lands. Our worker stages the raw file, then transforms it into indexed chunks. Batch ingestion processes groups of files. A streaming pipeline reacts to continually arriving events. Consider Kafka or Azure Event Hubs for replayable event streams with multiple consumers. Azure Data Factory can coordinate batch imports from existing systems when its connector and scheduling model fit. Microsoft also offers Data Factory in Microsoft Fabric for newer data integration workloads.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: A worker saves chunks and crashes before acknowledging a job. When the job is delivered again, inspect the job key, lease or delivery count, and active document version. Expect one published version when the retry completes. If the index contains duplicate chunks, check the uniqueness constraint and whether every attempt used the same version and chunk identifiers.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Watch the age of the oldest pending job, attempts per job, chunk count, pages rejected and time to searchable. Sample output for parse quality. Backpressure should limit new work when database or embedding capacity is exhausted. Schedule bulk reindexing separately from interactive answer traffic.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can move ingestion to a durable worker and make duplicate delivery harmless. Next: Track model and prompt changes

PostgreSQL locking clauses, Azure Service Bus queues, Azure Event Hubs, Azure Data Factory

docs.title: Track model and prompt changes
docs.text:
Track the data, retrieval settings, prompts, and model used to produce a quality score. Reproduce the result before promoting a change.

Core · 75 minutes · Prerequisites Choose a model and serving strategy and Cite sources and evaluate RAG.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A retrieval experiment improved recall last week. Today nobody can tell whether the gain came from the embedding model, chunk size, corpus, or evaluation questions. Save enough metadata to compare like with like.

docs.title: Record an experiment
docs.text:
A run groups the parameters, metrics and artifacts from one execution. The following optional MLflow example uses the same three labeled retrieval cases as the RAG chapter. Run it from the project root in an environment with python -m pip install "mlflow>=3,<4" installed. Save it as track_experiment.py in that root.

import mlflow

from examples.retrieval import retrieve

cases = [
    ("headset returns", "training", "returns-v1#1"),
    ("standard shipping", "training", "shipping-v1#1"),
    ("headset returns", "partner", "partner-v1#1"),
]
mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:///assistant-experiments.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("document-assistant")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_params({"dataset": "policies-v1", "retriever": "lexical", "k": 1})
    hits = sum(
        source in {chunk.id for chunk in retrieve(query, owner, limit=1)}
        for query, owner, source in cases
    )
    mlflow.log_metric("recall_at_1", hits / len(cases))
    print(f"Recall@1: {hits / len(cases):.2f}")

Run python track_experiment.py. It creates or updates the local tracking database and records recall of 1.00. On a clean environment it may also create an artifacts directory. For an application run, record the corpus revision, embedding deployment, prompts, selected chat deployment, input mix, and evaluator version.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: Add the “refund headphones” case. Expect recall to drop to 0.75. Change the dataset parameter to policies-v2 so comparisons show that the benchmark changed. If the metrics differ between two runs with the same labels, verify the referenced dataset contents, pipeline code and dependency versions before attributing improvement to the model.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Evaluate candidate changes offline before release. Use limited online traffic to test latency and real input distributions once offline gates pass. Version artifacts and settings so operations can trace a release to its experiment. Track adoption, quality and cost after promotion. Azure Machine Learning managed online endpoints are an option when serving a model you package. Foundry hosted model deployments fit the main architecture when a managed API meets the requirement. Both still need change control and evaluation.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You defined an experiment record that connects an AI release to its evidence. Next: Review the production design

MLflow Tracking, Azure Machine Learning online endpoints

docs.title: Observe quality, latency and cost
docs.text:
Trace a single answer from HTTP through retrieval to inference. Pick measurements that tell you why quality or latency changed.

Core · 70 minutes · Prerequisites Cite sources and evaluate RAG and Stream an answer.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Users report that answers are slower and sometimes unsupported. One log line showing 200 cannot tell which dependency was slow or whether the answer was grounded.

docs.title: Understand the signals
docs.text: A log records an event. A metric aggregates numerical observations. A trace links work across components, and a span describes one operation within it. Send a request or trace ID across the API and worker boundary so an operator can relate events without placing private content in logs.

docs.title: Read a trace
docs.text:
The synthetic trace below describes one successful answer. Nested spans may overlap, so compare their boundaries instead of adding every duration.

trace 63c2  POST /answers          1350 ms  status=200
  embed_query                       130 ms
  retrieve                          30 ms  candidates=3
  generate                        1160 ms  first_token=610 ms
                                               input_tokens=850 output_tokens=93

Generation dominates this trace. Use aggregate histograms to find out whether that pattern holds at p50 and p95. First-token time captures when streaming starts. End-to-end time captures completion. Record model deployment, prompt version, retrieval strategy and status with stable, low-cardinality tags. Keep request IDs in traces or logs, since using them as metric labels creates a separate series for each request.

docs.title: Extend and debug
docs.text: At 10:00, p95 latency rises and model 429 responses increase. Retrieval latency and database connections stay steady. Start with model concurrency, provider quota, and retries. Check if retries amplify request volume. Limit concurrency or fail gracefully under a deadline and verify that p95 and successful answers recover. If retrieval scores or authorized candidate counts drop too, inspect indexing and filters separately.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Set alerts that map to action, such as sustained error rate or document queue age. Track tokens and estimate cost with the input and output rates of the deployed model. Confirm estimates against billing and keep usage budgets. Use Azure Monitor and Application Insights to correlate traces and platform signals. Record metadata by default and review any policy to sample prompt or document content before enabling it.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can follow evidence from one trace to aggregate latency, errors, quality, and cost. Next: Measure performance and cache results

OpenTelemetry signals, Application Insights OpenTelemetry

docs.title: Measure performance and cache results
docs.text:
Estimate concurrency, choose a low-risk cache, and work out whether another API replica would help.

Core · 70 minutes · Prerequisites Observe quality, latency and cost.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: At peak load, Document Assistant spends money embedding repeated questions and waiting for model capacity. Scaling API containers may leave the provider bottleneck unchanged.

docs.title: Measure the bottleneck
docs.text: If 12 requests per second each spend an average of two seconds in flight, expect about 24 concurrent requests under steady load. Compare that estimate with measured p95 latency, provider limits, connection pool, and worker counts. Test realistic query mixes, including streaming and cold requests. Batching embeddings can increase throughput and add a wait before a batch is sent.

docs.title: Sketch a cache
docs.text:
Redis can hold computed embeddings under a key with a time to live (TTL). Begin with a key that incorporates scope, embedding deployment version, and an HMAC of the exact embedding input. An HMAC uses a secret to generate the digest, so the key need not expose the original question.

Request Result with a 300-second TTL Tenant A, model v1, question Q, time 0 Miss and compute Tenant A, model v1, Q, time 30 Hit Tenant B, model v1, Q, time 30 Miss because the scope differs Tenant A, model v2, Q, time 30 Miss because the model version differs Tenant A, model v1, Q, time 310 Miss after expiry

This cache holds embeddings. Retrieval still enforces document access. Caching entire answers needs a stronger key with corpus and permission versions because documents and access can change.

docs.title: Practice and debugging
docs.text: Traffic doubles. CPU stays low while model rate limits and database pool waits rise. Explain why adding API replicas can raise pressure on both dependencies. Introduce bounded model concurrency, review retries and consider a separately scaled worker. Verify p95, throughput, provider errors, and cache hit rate on the same load profile.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Treat a cache as a performance dependency. Tune its deadline and define how to fall back when it fails. Measure memory, expiry, and stale results. If a single miss triggers a burst of duplicate work, combine concurrent refreshes or stagger expirations. Use Azure Managed Redis when a managed cache is justified. Microsoft's retirement guidance covers the older Azure Cache for Redis service.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You can choose which work to cache and distinguish scaling an API from scaling its dependencies. Next: Scale ingestion with queues and workers

Redis EXPIRE, Azure Redis retirement guidance

docs.title: Review the production design
docs.text:
Review a production design for Document Assistant. Use the earlier code and exercises as evidence, and turn failure cases into concrete release and incident decisions.

Core · 120 minutes · Prerequisites The RAG, approval, Azure, delivery, and production operations chapters.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Two teams want to ask questions about policy documents. A released assistant must cite the policy version a user can access and pause before saving a note. The teams need a way to publish new policy versions and verify that users see the change.

docs.title: Draw the request and ingestion paths
docs.text:
Use Container Apps for the API and worker. Use Blob Storage for document bytes, PostgreSQL with pgvector for authorized search and job state, and Microsoft Foundry deployments for model requests. Use Entra user identity at the API boundary and workload identities for service connections. The diagram is a proposed topology. Region, network and permissions belong in an environment-specific design.

flowchart LR
    U["User"] -->|Entra token| A["Document Assistant API"]
    A -->|Upload bytes| B["Blob Storage"]
    A -->|Queue and authorized retrieval| P["PostgreSQL + pgvector"]
    A -->|Generate a cited answer| F["Foundry"]
    P -->|Claim job| W["Ingestion worker"]
    B -->|Read source| W
    W -->|Embed chunks| F
    W -->|Publish version| P
    A --> M["Azure Monitor"]
    W --> M

Describe how a validated request reaches retrieval, how citation lookup reuses the same access rules, and when a pending proposal becomes a saved note. Explain how the worker makes a new document version searchable without exposing a partially written index.

docs.title: Gather sample evidence
docs.text:
Run the following from the project root. Use the results alongside the earlier unauthorized-caller and invalid-input exercises.

python -m examples.evaluation
python -m examples.agent
python -m examples.approvals

For the seeded training data expect recall@1 of 1.00, a cited 30-day returns answer, abstention for the missing warranty policy, and zero notes before approval. Repeating approval should leave one note.

Define a stronger held-out benchmark for a release. Include exact terms, paraphrases, missing answers, outdated policies, and conflicts between teams. Example gates for a real design review are zero cross-team data leaks, zero unapproved writes, recall@5 of at least 90% across held-out answerable queries, and p95 response time under three seconds on a declared load profile. Confirm the thresholds with the users and adjust them if the actual workload requires it.

docs.title: Rehearse a release and incident
docs.text:
Situation Evidence to inspect Recovery and check An upload never becomes searchable Document status, oldest job, attempts, parse result Requeue the same version after fixing the cause. Check that exactly one version is searchable. Model latency rises and requests receive 429 Provider quota, retries, model concurrency, trace timings Reduce concurrency or shed load. Verify retries and p95 settle before restoring traffic. A new revision cites an old policy Revision, prompt, deployment and index versions Restore traffic to the last compatible revision. Check the citation and verify the current schema still works with it.

For a failed authorization case, pause the affected path, preserve diagnostic evidence, assess which users and records were affected, and rerun the isolation checks after a fix.

docs.title: Design review deliverables
docs.text: Write a short architecture decision record and include your two request paths, identity and permission map, versioned release inputs, evaluation results, and incident checklist. Include estimated costs and a cleanup plan for any future Azure environment. Explain which workload metric would justify a new search service, broker or cache, and who would own it. Confirm a second reader can reproduce the sample checks and explain the first action for each incident.

docs.title: Recap and next step
docs.text:
You reviewed the full lifecycle of an AI application, from request validation and citations through Azure releases and incident response. Back to the roadmap

Azure Well-Architected Framework, Azure Architecture Center
